#4758. Two Sides of Human Nature: Why We Become Angels or Devils

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Many countries and regions are affected by war, violence, and social unrest in the world. These regions typically also face extremely serious living and economic conditions. Conversely, in richer nations with more favorable conditions, people adhere more closely to ethical standards, the law, and human principles. A prime example is the countries of Northern Europe, which experience lower rates of crime and political unrest than many other nations and consistently rank among the happiest in the world [1]. It is striking that these countries, due to harsh climatic conditions and difficult access to resources, have at times had a history marked entirely by war, violence, and malevolence.

The dual nature of human beings has been a subject of religion, mysticism, philosophy, and ethics throughout history. These schools of thought have acknowledged an animalistic dimension—characterized by malice, selfishness, deceit, envy, violence, and greed—alongside a dimension that aspires toward transcendence, defined by generosity, kindness, and self-sacrifice. At times, individuals may even surrender their own lives—the most fundamental instinct of all living creatures—for others or higher values. Religious traditions attribute the root of this duality to the unique creation of the human species. From this perspective, humans, like other animals, possess a physical body rooted in the Earth, driven by an instinctive desire for survival and a craving to secure greater access to food, water, and warm, safe shelter protected from predators.

The lives of our ancestors were largely spent in harsh and unforgiving environments, where survival was naturally the main priority. This response is also observed in many other animals. Much of what we now classify as moral vices actually consisted of behaviors aimed at individual survival and the acquisition of resources. However, in less hostile conditions—and when well-fed and at peace—humans become tamer; they begin to attend to the needs and suffering of others, prioritizing family and tribe but extending concern even to more distant fellow human beings. In such a state, humans develop a desire to understand the world, engage in artistic creation, and reflect on the universe around them.

Religions offer precepts and rituals to bring the animalistic nature under control and allow the transcendent dimension to flourish. Yet the malevolent aspect of human nature has, at times, even exploited religion to serve selfish, animalistic desires. Throughout history, countless wars and acts of bloodshed have unfolded under the guise of religion.

For centuries, humans have considered themselves superior to other living beings due to their intelligence. However, a systematic review has shown that many abilities once thought to be “uniquely human”—such as tool-making, planning, and problem-solving—are also present, to some extent, in other animals. Nevertheless, humans exhibit exceptionally strong capabilities in areas such as recalling the past and imagining the future, tool use, problem-solving, social cognition, and communication. No single trait exclusive to humans can account for this superiority; this applies even to distinct capacities like language. We do not possess a single “magical” trait, nor has culture alone shaped us. Rather, our abilities reinforce one another—a synergy evident in both child development and the co-evolution of genes and culture [2].

It appears that the root of human superiority and behavior originates largely from the human brain’s larger and more complex cerebral cortex. The structure and genetics of this brain region are distinctly different from those of our close primate relatives, such as chimpanzees; they also exhibit significant differences compared to Neanderthals and even our own ancestors from thousands of years ago. This enables our species—through the expansion of collective culture—to obtain a more distinctly human standard for living. However, this region does not always exert complete control over the lower brain centers responsible for governing vital instincts (3).

When we are hungry, exposed to freezing conditions, have failed in competition for a mate, or face the threat of predation by animals or other humans, our sympathetic nervous system—the “fight-or-flight” mechanism—is instinctively activated. This system triggers metabolic changes to supply necessary fuel, modulates the immune system to combat infections and physical injuries, and induces cardiovascular responses to help us cope with these conditions. Psychologically, it generates stress and anxiety, activating specific brain regions such as the amygdala.

The amygdala disrupts the interaction between the higher brain centers—the neocortex—and the lower, more primitive structures. Consequently, the brain shifts toward rapid, instinctive decision-making, bypassing the slower, more deliberate, and effortful processes of reflection. In this state, an individual temporarily loses the capacity for analytical thinking and self-critique; instead, the brain’s primary function becomes making instinctive choices aimed at survival. Under these circumstances, moral priorities fade into the background [4].

However, given recent advancements in neuroscience, dividing the brain into “higher” human regions and “lower” animalistic ones is an oversimplification. In 1960, Paul D. MacLean proposed the “triune brain” theory—three distinct components: the reptilian brain, the limbic system, and the neocortex. He attributed instinctive behaviors like territoriality, dominance, mating, and deception primarily to the reptilian brain, suggesting these components operate largely independently.

In recent decades, however, this theory has faced significant criticism. We now understand the brain as an interconnected network, not a collection of independent layers. Emotions and cognition are deeply intertwined, and no single region can be considered solely responsible for any complex behavior [5].

Human beings possess remarkable capacities for cooperation, compassion, and creativity, as well as powerful tendencies toward self-preservation, competition, and aggression. Which of these tendencies becomes dominant depends not only on our evolutionary heritage and brain organization but also on the psychological, social, and environmental conditions in which we live. Harsh conditions often breed greater violence and depravity, potentially turning affected societies into a “geopolitical ulcer” that creates challenges for other nations as well. Such circumstances may also drive individuals toward misery, crime, and lawlessness.

Furthermore, the political strategies of powerful countries—which undermine the welfare, education, healthcare, and housing of targeted nations—can distort the human values within those communities. Ultimately, these actions will return to haunt the perpetrators, much like a boomerang. Still, cruelty does not always arise from bad conditions; sometimes dangerous beliefs, using our finest mental capacities, can produce violence and chaos even in comfortable circumstances.

1. https://data.un.org/DocumentData.aspx?id=505#1

2. Laland K, Seed A. Understanding Human Cognitive Uniqueness. Annu Rev Psychol. 2021 Jan 4;72:689-716.

3. Namba T, Huttner WB. What Makes Us Human: Insights from the Evolution and Development of the Human Neocortex. Annu Rev Cell Dev Biol. 2024 Oct;40(1):427-452.

4. Schwabe L. Memory under stress: from single systems to network changes. Eur J Neurosci. 2017 Feb;45(4):478-489.

5. MacLean, P. D. (1990). The Triune Brain in Evolution: Role in Paleocerebral Functions. Springer.

#4757. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4755. Tokyo police consider using AI to reconstruct traffic accidents

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:07 AM EST

One law enforcement agency in Japan reportedly wants to make something normally confined to sci-fi crime thrillers a reality: interactive, AI-powered reconstructions of real-world accidents. According to The Japan Times, Tokyo’s Metropolitan Department is developing a system that combines AI with security camera footage and 3D spatial data captured by camera-equipped mapping vehicles to digitally reconstruct traffic accidents. Investigators using the tool would reportedly be able to measure vehicle speeds and distances on a screen and replay the event in simulation from multiple perspectives, including overhead or even through the eyes of a nearby driver or pedestrian.

That’s the goal, at least. Details about how this proposed system will actually work remain sparse, though the report says that the police plan to begin testing in June 2027 and potentially launch full operations in January 2028. In theory, digital reconstructions could reduce the need for labor-intensive physical, on-site inspections (the current approach) which can close off roads for ours and lead to traffic jams.

However, AI reconstructions bring risks of their own, especially if they rely on generative AI tools that are prone to hallucinating fabricated data. In the United States  and elsewhere, courts are struggling to reign in examples of inaccurate, AI-generated court filings and police reports. The use of AI-enhanced video and audio and even deepfake clones presented in trials are also forcing the legal system to reevaluate how it treats algorithm-altered evidence.

As far as we can tell, the Tokyo police proposal would be the first systematic use of an AI reconstruction for traffic assessments. In 2024, law enforcement in Pune, India, east of Mumbai, reportedly considered using an AI-enabled “digital reconstruction” to analyze a high profile drunk driving incident that killed two pedestrians. But it’s unclear whether that system was ever actually realized or used in court.

Researchers have been exploring the underlying technology for such a system for years. In July, a team from the Technical University of Munich and the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office in Germany showed off an AI system they say is capable of compiling thousands of photographers from a crime scene to create a digital reconstruction. In that case, the team said the system could automatically identify and classify objects in the scene. Investigators could then virtually go in and query the 3D crime scene to try and collect and analyze evidence long after the actual event occurred.

Meanwhile, researchers at Hasselt University in Belgium, are also in the early stage of developing a tool aiming to use multimodal language models for digital reconstructions which they say could aid law enforcement and insurers.

Generative AI tools are also creating new headaches for the legal system. Hundreds of lawyers around the globe have been sanctioned by courts for filling legal briefs with bogus, hallucinated case law. In June, a judge in Mississippi canceled a civil trial’s proceedings after all four lawyers on opposing sides of the case were caught citing a fake, AI-generated court filing. And citations are not the only issue. A growing number of police departments in the U.S. are using AI tools to analyze evidence and draft police reports, which the American Civil Liberty Union warns “removes important human elements from police procedures.”

At least partially AI-generated evidence, like the kind that many result from a digital reconstitution, has already appeared in some legal proceedings. In 2024, a Washington State judge overseeing a murder case barred the defendant’s lawyers from introducing cellphone footage that had been digitally enhanced using AI software. According to court filings at the time, the judge in that case worried that admitting that AI- enhanced footage could “lead to a confusion of the issue and muddling of eyewitness testimony.”

The core tension here, and with other uses of AI as evidence, is whether or not the AI system can be trusted to accurately reflect reality. An AI system reconstructing traffic scenes, though potentially  less higher stages than a murder trial, may nonetheless face similar headwinds.

#4754. DARVO at Work: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Simone had done everything right. She had led her department's most impactful projects, trained half the team, and been told twice that she was "next in line" for a senior manager role.

Then the promotion went to Mark. He had been with the company for about a year, created extra work for others by turning in slop, and, as nearly everyone knew, had been in a relationship with their boss, Jody, for the last 6 months.

Simone didn't accuse anyone of anything. She politely asked HR whether the promotion process had been reviewed for a conflict of interest. Before long, Simone was labeled "a troublemaker," and somehow Jody was a victim of "harassment about her private life."

How does the person who raised a legitimate concern end up as the problem, while the person who created the problem ends up as the victim?

Jennifer Freyd (1997) coined the term DARVO— for Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender—to describe how people often respond when confronted about wrongdoing. It was first studied in the context of domestic violence and abuse, but it occurs anywhere accountability is brought up, including the workplace.

DARVO can be deliberate and calculated, or reflexive and emotion-driven. Either way, the person who dared to speak up is vilified. Here’s how it might have played out with Simone and Jody.

The organization's attention switches to protecting Jody and Mark, the people with power, and away from advocating for Simone, someone originally harmed by that power. And the original concern, a manager granting a promotion to her lover in violation of conflict-of-interest policy, has disappeared from the conversation. It’s now about "You are attacking my private life and hurting my feelings."

DARVO is used so often because it is effective. Research shows it. In a 2020 set of experiments, people read the same incident with or without the accused person's DARVO response. When DARVO was present, readers judged the victim as less believable and more to blame, and the perpetrator as less responsible (Harsey & Freyd, 2020).

DARVO can also gaslight the original target. Harsey, Zurbriggen, and Freyd (2017) found that the more DARVO people encountered when confronting someone who had wronged them, the more they blamed themselves. Self-blame can lead to self-silencing, and Simone might come to wonder if she really is "just bitter" and should say nothing.

From the inside, DARVO can spur confusion. Simone starts editing her own memory: Was her tone too sharp? Did she misread something? Was she, deep down, just jealous? Each doubt could make sense, and that’s what makes them dangerous. Over time, that self-doubt can harden into silence—a coping strategy that may cost you who you are. So, if you find yourself wondering whether you were the problem, keep asking yourself: What actually happened first?

Research also offers some good news: People who were taught to recognize the DARVO pattern were less swayed by it. They saw the victim as more credible and the perpetrator as less so. Simply knowing the pattern's name weakens its grip (Harsey & Freyd, 2020). Of course, recognizing the pattern requires paying attention. The clearest signal is a subject change. If a question about a decision turns into complaints about the questioner's tone, personality, or propriety, ask why.

DARVO succeeds by making us forget the original question. In Simone's case, it was simple: Was there a conflict of interest? Everything that followed—the denials, the attacks on Simone, Jody's claims of being a victim—was meant to bury it.

Do not be distracted. Hold on to the original concern. Keep asking “what happened first.” And insist on the resolution of the original question.

Freyd, J. J. (1997). Violations of power, adaptive blindness, and betrayal trauma theory. Feminism & Psychology, 7(1), 22–32.

Harsey, S., & Freyd, J. J. (2020). Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender (DARVO): What Is the Influence on Perceived Perpetrator and Victim Credibility? Journal of Aggression, Maltreatment & Trauma, 29(8), 897–916.

Harsey, S., Zurbriggen, E. L., & Freyd, J. J. (2017). Perpetrator responses to victim confrontation: DARVO and victim self-blame. Journal of Aggression, Maltreatment & Trauma, 26, 644–663.

#4753. Meta-backed 250 MW solar farm breaks ground in Arkansas

Arkansas is getting another 250 megawatts (MW) of solar power, and Meta has signed up to buy it.

EDP Renewables North America (EDPR NA) broke ground on Cypress Knee Solar in Chicot County, in the southeastern corner of the state, on November 4. The solar farm is expected to be completed by 2028, bringing several hundred construction jobs and an estimated $25 million in county revenue over its lifetime.

Meta’s long-term power purchase agreement helps it work toward its pledge to match 100% of its annual electricity use with renewable energy generation. Don’t confuse that pledge with Meta powering its data centers with renewables around the clock, though – Facebook and Instagram’s parent company is also backing new gas plants to meet its growing power demand.

The companies announced the deal in May. Cypress Knee is their third clean-energy agreement, bringing the total capacity covered by Meta’s deals with EDPR NA to 545 MW.

“As energy demand continues to rise, projects like Cypress Knee Solar help strengthen grid reliability while creating jobs, generating meaningful local revenue, and delivering long-term benefits to the communities that host them,” said EDPR NA CEO Sandhya Ganapathy.

EDPR NA says it has already contributed more than $77,000 during project development, including money to restore the Lakeside High School greenhouse, resources for the Lakeside Robotics team, and funding for the Lake Village food pantry.

#4752. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Kia’s Sportage-sized electric SUV, the EV5, was spotted with a distinct new style and an overhauled interior, including a huge widescreen infotainment screen.

The EV5 is the fully electric SUV we want, but can’t have in the US. After launching it in China in 2023, Kia introduced the global version last year, which is now on sale in Europe, Canada, the UK, and other markets.

It has already been a big part of Kia’s comeback in China and is expected to become one of its best-selling EVs.

Kia appears to be preparing an updated version. A new EV5 model was recently spotted by ShortsCar in a South Korean parking garage without camouflage, and it’s expected to be the updated version.

You can see in the video that the design has changed quite a bit. Up front, the hood and headlights remain about the same, but new design elements like a black accent light are added.

It also features a unique bumper design, similar to that of the rugged EV5 WKNDR Concept Kia revealed last November at the Guangzhou Motor Show.

The biggest changes are inside, where the interior appears to be completely overhauled. Instead of the current large display screen spanning from the driver to the center, the new EV5 features a display that extends from the center to the passenger side.

#4750. 1,500 years ago, a man trekked across Europe as the Roman Empire fell

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:56 AM EST

If you were going to live in Europe at any point in time, word of advice: Avoid the fifth century. The mighty Roman Empire was floundering. Attila the Hun repeatedly invaded the eastern Roman Empire, and even Italy in the year 452 CE. Fierce Germanic forces known as the Visigoths and Vandals sacked and raided Rome, first in 410 and again in 455. The Franks (in present-day France, Belgium, and western Germany) were busy wresting control in the west. And in 476, the entire Roman Empire collapsed. Put simply, it was a rough century.

With all of that upheaval, many people picked up and left their homes, undoubtedly in search of better, more stable places to live. Historians call the period between the fourth and seventh centuries in Europe as the Migration Period since so many people were on the move.

Now, thanks to some 1,500-year-old DNA from an elaborate ship burial in northwestern Germany, we are tantalizingly close to understanding one man’s journey from one end of the Roman Empire to the other. Oh, and he also had leprosy.

This grueling, potentially 800-mile-long journey is detailed in a study published in this month’s edition of the journal iScience.

Discovered in the 1990s, the Fallward burial ground is a treasure trove of information from the Migration Period. Located on coastal marshland, about 20 miles west of Hamburg, Germany, the cemetery contains about 200 cremation burials and 60 graves from the end of the third to the late fifth century. Many of the graves were dug deep into damp clay, which has helped preserve many striking finds.

One of the most remarkable graves is simply labeled as site 265. The grave belongs to an approximately 50-year-old man, who died sometime between 425 and 450. The man probably rowed or fished along the German coast since his skeletal remains indicate his upper arm muscles were well developed. He was also buried inside a 13-foot-long oak boat covered with wooden panels that formed a roof-like structure.

But the boat burial isn’t the only thing that makes grave 265 unique.

“The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest; these included a chair, artfully decorated and carved from an alder trunk. Furthermore, the man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances,” explained Dr. Hauke Jöns from the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research in Wilhelmshaven, Germany, explained in a statement on the new findings.

The elaborate chair was presumably painted and is often referred to as a throne. Far from an ordinary piece of furniture meant for daily use, it was instead a symbol of the authority the deceased wielded in life.

The late Roman military belt perhaps raises the most questions about who the man buried in 265 was. The belt shows signs of both use and repair. While its presence doesn’t necessarily mean the man was a soldier in the Roman military—he could’ve acquired it through trade, inheritance, or as war booty—it also doesn’t mean he wasn’t a soldier for Rome. If he was, he would have likely been part of the foederati. These warriors served Rome through a treaty, or foedus, rather than as Roman citizens.

The grave also included: a stool carved with a hunting scene and inscription, a game board, a ceramic vessel, and a bronze basin.

For nearly 30 years, archaeologists could only speculate about what these grave goods meant about who was buried in grave 265. But with the new DNA analysis, we now have some concrete answers about who this man was. Though the team was able to extract DNA from three individuals from the Fallward burial ground, “the results were particularly striking” for the man in 265. The new genetic analysis confirms two things about the man.

First, he was from or had close family from the Danube region in the eastern part of the Roman Empire, which comprised parts of modern day Croatia, Hungary, Slovenia, and Serbia. That’s a long way from his grave in northwestern Germany, so at some point he or a close relative traveled more than 800 miles, leaving behind the Roman Empire in process. Second, he had a rare form of leprosy.

“Leprosy is a chronic disease. It can take years for clear symptoms to appear. The man had not yet suffered any bone damage. Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease,” explained study co-author Dr. Almut Nebel from the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Christian-Albrechts-University in Kiel, Germany.

Study co-author Dr. Ben Krause-Kyora (also at IKMB) speculates, “He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers, which run on either side of Fallward]. Or he might have undertaken long journeys as a trader.”

Either way, the man in grave 265 likely lived through a heck of a lot before taking up fishing on the rural German coastline.

#4749. Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes at 50% off used

Once America’s most popular electric pickup, the Ford F-150 Lightning is finding a second life on the used market.

The F-150 Lightning is hard to pass up at 50% to 60% off sticker price, even used. With new models no longer available, Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes on the used market.

After the last model rolled off the assembly line last December, CEO Jim Farley said the decision to end production came as the “very high-end EVs, the $50K, 70K, $80,000 vehicles, they just weren’t selling.”

At 50% to 60% off, it now looks like a bargain in the used market. “When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” Jimmy Douglas, CEO of Plug, a wholesale EV dealer, recently told Bloomberg.

On the used market, however, “the Lightning is 50% to 60% of the sticker price and that is really a sweet spot,” he added.

Used Ford F-150 Lightnings are selling in about 20 days, less than half the 44-day average for used vehicles in the US. According to Edmunds.com, prices are now up 4% to about $50,000 since the start of the year.

Douglass said that close to one-third of used models are sold by rival dealerships that would normally flip them back to Ford. However, many are opting to sell them directly because of demand.

Chase Norris from Colorado called the electric pickup a bargain. He purchased a used Lightning for around $40,000 and considers it a major upgrade from his previous gas F-150.

EV Group CEO and cofounder Alex Lawrence, which sells pre-owned electric vehicles, said he can’t get his hands on any reasonably priced used F-150 Lightnings currently.

He said many Lightning buyers use it as a second truck to save money during their weekly commute.

It looks essentially the same as the gas-powered F-150, offers instant torque, and produces zero tailpipe emissions, but the electric pickup failed to meet Ford’s expectations because of its higher price.

The base F-150 Lightning Pro debuted in 2021 with a starting MSRP of $39,974, but that was quickly raised to around $60,000 a year or so later.

According to Edmunds.com, the average transaction price for the F-150 Lightning in its first year of sales was $79,000 because Ford focused on higher-priced trims. The gas version’s ATP was about $19,000 less.

Even with the higher sticker price, Ford was losing a considerable amount on each Lightning it produced. In Q1 2024, Ford lost more than $100,000 on every EV it built.

Next year, Ford will take another crack at the electric pickup market with the Fathom, the first vehicle based on its “groundbreaking” new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform.

Ford said the Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard-range version. Even with the $1,595 delivery fee included, the electric pickup will start at under $30,000.

As the first vehicle built on its UEV platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step-change from its first-generation EVs.

According to Ford, the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4 and will be the first vehicle with Apple Maps directly integrated into the navigation system.

We also know the electric pickup will have a NACS port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger this summer.

Ford reportedly aims to sell around 100,000 Fathoms in its first year. CEO Jim Farley said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week that the launch remains on track for Q4 2027.

Farley called the Fathom a “breakthrough product” and said that the MSRP under $30,000 is perfect for today’s market.

At least some F-150 owners are already trading in for lower-priced options. A member of the Ford F-150 Lightning Owners Group, JF, said that although it was a great ride, “Carvana gave us just a little less than we paid new,” adding, “R2, here we come!”

When Torque News reached out, JF said he “really liked the Lightning,” but wanted something smaller. “With the current increase in resale value, the time to trade seemed right,” JF added.

The Rivian R2 (see our review) Performance with the Launch Package is now available to order starting at $57,990 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 330 miles and 656 hp. The R2 Premium will go on sale later this year, starting at $53,990

In Spring 2027, Rivian will launch the R2 Standard, starting at $44,990 with an estimated range of up to 275 miles and 350 hp.

So were they losing $100k / truck, or the average loss when all development was included ended up being $100k? Big difference. I don't believe the cost to build each one was $170k+. That makes no sense. They just priced them too high to amortize the development costs over enough vehicles to make them profitable. Every vehicle has to sell a minimum # before they start to make a profit.

Surging F-150 Lightning sales on the used market show buyers want electric pickups. But at the right price.

At $60,000 to $70,000, the Lightning wasn’t so attractive, but at $40,000 used, it suddenly is. Perhaps Ford is on to something with its next-gen EV pickup, the Fathom, set to go on sale starting at under $30,000.

Will it deliver on its promise? Ford has yet to reveal battery specs, towing capacity, range, or any other specs. We should learn more soon.

#4748. What the Recent Tech Outage Can Teach Us About Balance

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

As I write this, parts of North America and Europe are experiencing a Microsoft outage that is affecting certain parts of the cloud infrastructure, particularly office communication services such as Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 360. While this is certainly causing disruption and inconvenience in many corporate and business settings, it may also be reminding us of an important reality that we often talk about but rarely implement: work-life balance.

In the United States, it has long been reported that workers struggle with creating healthy boundaries between their lives and their jobs, and a 2025 study found that a staggering 66 percent of American workers reported having experienced “some degree of burnout” in the past year (Robinson, 2025). Additionally, 2024 research indicated that 44 percent of employees and 53 percent of supervisors experienced burnout at their jobs (Malinsky, 2022). It is no secret that many of us struggle to find the “sweet spot” between work and the rest of our lives. Increasingly, this disparity between work and life is being seen as a larger problem that, according to a 2021 study, is more than “an individual-level phenomenon,” and is “a societal concern that necessitates systematic support from a wider range of stakeholders” (Fan, Yuyang, et al., 2021).

Along with the statistical evidence, we can find plenty of anecdotal proof that this is a widespread problem: you would be hard-pressed to find a person who does not report some level of exhaustion or burnout related to their career, myself and those I know being no exception. But if it is such an issue, why are we unable to see something like this Microsoft outage as a gift rather than an inconvenience? I would argue that it has to do with our longstanding relationship with work and our misprioritization of its importance. American attitudes about work have long been centered around productivity, busyness, results, and multitasking. Words like “balance” are simply not part of our career-related vernacular.

When something like a technology outage forces us to let go of our usual outcome-orientation towards our jobs, it can feel odd and somehow “wrong.” Looking at social media comments today, I am seeing more that speak to how annoying and inconvenient this outage is and less that speak to it allowing for a slower workday or an (albeit forced) opportunity to not work as hard. But perhaps we can learn from today’s widespread inconvenience. In some workplaces, you are unable to send or answer emails, communicate as usual, or access cloud-related platforms. In one sense, this is frustrating. In another, it is permission not to do these things that, let’s be honest, are often done from home, from the dinner table, at unhealthy hours, in the midst of other life activities, and at the cost of mindfulness and presence in our lives. I am not suggesting that tech outages are good for business, but rather that they can remind us that creating space between work and life is necessary for our overall well-being.

Sometimes inconveniences can be opportunities. In Buddhist philosophy, the concept that the “obstacle is the path” is applicable to today’s inconvenience. The obstacle (not being able to access the usual work platforms) is the path to allowing ourselves to slow down and create some space between work and life—at least for a day or two.

Bryan Robinson, Ph.D. “Job Burnout at 66% in 2025, New Study Shows.” Forbes, 8 Feb. 2025, www.forbes.com/sites/bryanrobinson/2025/02/08/job-burnout-at-66-in-2025…. Accessed 13 Nov. 2026.

Malinsky, Gili. “There’s More Than One Type of Work Burnout―How to Identify Which You Have.” CNBC, 29 Sept. 2022, www.cnbc.com/make-it/2022/09/29/theres-more-than-one-type-of-burnout-ho…. Accessed 13 Nov. 2026.

Fan, Yuyang, et al. “A Process‐Oriented, Multilevel, Multidimensional Conceptual Framework of Work–Life Balance Support: A Multidisciplinary Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Agenda.” International Journal of Management Reviews, vol. 23, no. 4, 5 May 2021, 10.1111/ijmr.12254.

#4747. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4745. E-quipment highlight: Jungheinrich launches new forklift for Asian markets

Like many equipment brands, German forklift maker Jungheinrich has been struggling to crack the Asian industrial markets – but the company is set to change all that with the launch of a new line of 1.6- to 3-ton class electric forklifts designed specifically to navigate the region’s tight warehouses and factories.

Jungheinrich launched the next generation of its EFG MB and MC electric counterbalance forklifts, giving businesses more flexibility to match truck performance with the battery options, charging systems, and operator features that meet their specific needs.

“Different operations have different requirements,” said Lisa Jing Xue, Managing Director at Jungheinrich’s Qingpu Plant, China. “With the EFG M series, customers can configure the (forklift) truck around their application, workload and operators – whether they need greater maneuverability for confined warehouse spaces, or a stable, powerful truck for demanding transport and stacking work.”

Forklift buyers can choose between two performance packages, prioritizing energy efficiency for everyday material handling or more driving and lifting muscle for more demanding, high-throughput operations. The higher-performance package comes standard on models rated for 2.5-3.0 tons, with a choice of either lead-acid or lithium-ion batteries with 346 or 690 Ah of capacity available to suit different workloads and shift patterns. Both ship with regenerative braking tech that can recover up to 30% of the energy used in stopping and lowering loads, too, helping to keep these machines running longer between charging sessions.

“We carried out extensive customer research to understand what the market needs,” added Jing Xue. “Customers can invest in the performance required today and add further capabilities as their application demands.”

Optional features include fingertip controls, a larger 4″ digital display, upgraded LED lighting, and operator-assistance (ADAS) systems, while flexible seating and cabin configurations are designed to keep drivers comfortable through long shifts. A slim B-pillar and glass roof help visibility in busy warehouses, while the four-wheel EFG MC gets automatic cornering speed reduction as standard. Integrated telematics are also standard, giving fleet managers access to utilization data, maintenance planning and pre-operational checks from day one.

Jungheinrich says the order books for both the three- and four-wheel electric forklifts are open now, ready to be supported by the company’s 6,000+ person strong service network across the Asia-Pacific region.

#4744. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4743. Janus Electric secures battery supply deal for its battery-swap semi truck

Australian conversion specialists Janus Electric have been celebrating a growing slate of orders for their Class 8 electric truck conversions, which ditch diesel in favor of advanced battery-swap electric power – but exactly how they’d deliver all those trucks was still a question. Now, we have an answer: Electrovaya will supply the batteries.

The concept of dropping an electric power unit into a Class 8 semi makes perfect sense, as most of these trucks are built as gliders. That is, rolling body and chassis without an engine and transmission that’s ready to receive power from Cummins, Detroit, International, or Volvo Penta. That’s the role that Janus Electric sees itself occupying, and it seems to be working.

Janus’ reservation book crept past 70 units this past summer, helped along in part by California’s HVIP Program and the US EPA’s Diesel Emission Reduction Act (DERA) Grants. When the HVIP voucher is combined with the Port of Los Angeles’ “Plus” support, customers can received up to $166,000 per truck conversion. Factor in the massive fuel savings of electric and the classic good looks of square-nose Western Star truck body, and it’s easy to see why they’d be a popular choice.

As Jerry Seinfeld taught us however, it’s one thing to take a reservation – it’s another thing to deliver. To help make it happen, Janus has inked a battery supply deal with Electrovaya that will see a $26 million initial purchase orders for Electrovaya battery packs to demand for Janus’ products in the US and Canada, along with the battery company purchasing approximately $1.4 million in Janus stock with (what seems to be) actual money.

“Electrovaya is an important partner to Janus Electric, and we’re particularly pleased it has decided to invest directly in our business,” explains Ben Hutt, Managing Director and CEO of Janus Electric. “The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport.”

The Janus Electric-repowered trucks carry a stout, 480 hp electric motor drawing power from a standard 310 kWh battery pack, with up to two battery packs (one on each side) of the truck. In practice, that gives the Janus trucks up to 370 miles of loaded range. After that, the batteries can be DC fast charged in under 90 minutes, or swapped for fresh ones in about four minutes without too much in the way of specialized equipment. That’s not just Janus’ killer app, it means that a battery supply deal like this one with a strategic partner who’s invested in the fledgling company’s success is such a huge deal.

“Reliable battery supply is critical to our growth,” adds Hutt, “and Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale. Both companies see considerable opportunity in this market, and we look forward to building on our partnership.”

For their part, Electrovoya executives seem to know their role here, and seem excited to be a part of what Janus is doing. “Class 8 trucking is one of the most exciting and demanding frontiers in electrification, and Janus has demonstrated real commercial traction with fleets in the US, Canada and Australia,” said Dr. Raj Das Gupta, CEO of Electrovaya. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations.”

Electrovaya will be expanding its American manufacturing capacity with lithium-ion cell, module, and battery pack production at its new, potentially BABA-compliant facility in Jamestown, New York, which is expected to come online in 2027.

#4742. How Gossip Is Good for Us

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

As the saying goes, “If you don’t have anything good to say, don’t say anything.” But in the words of Alice Roosevelt Longworth, perhaps more of us prefer: “If you can’t say something good about someone, sit right here by me.” After all, deep down, we all love some good gossip, don’t we?

In fact, by some estimates of everyday conversations, upwards of 65 percent of what we talk about involves people and social interactions, both self-disclosures and information about others’ escapades. And “gossip,” defined as the telling of stories about the everyday adventures of the people in our lives that we tell to, with, and about others, began deep in our evolutionary history. As soon as we began to use language, we started to gossip!

As we gather around the holiday table this year with friends and family we may not have seen in a while, we will share stories of our lives, stories of their lives, and stories of our friends and family not able to be present at the table. The good news is that this is actually good for us. Whereas gossip has a bad reputation, in fact, it serves a critical function in weaving our lives together and keeping our social groups connected.

Dunbar, an evolutionary anthropologist, argues that gossip began very early in our ancestral history. Living in larger social groups benefited our survival, and gossip is a necessary part of keeping larger social groups cohesive. Through sharing stories about how Uncle Joe and Aunt Louise are settling into their new living arrangements in Timbuktu, we maintain a sense of belonging to the group, and this sense of belonging adds to our own sense of meaning and purpose in life. When we feel socially isolated, we actually experience physical pain; Williams and Nida show experimentally that social exclusion for as little as two minutes leads to physiological pain responses and emotional distress, and longer periods of social isolation can result in depression, helplessness, and alienation. Maintaining social connections by integrating our lives with others through stories and gossip brings us together and creates a sense of well-being.

Gossip also serves to help us with advice and discussion of possible problems—if you are thinking about changing jobs, a story about cousin Bill who just did that could provide invaluable information as you consider your options. With my colleagues David Pillemer and Dorthe Thomsen, we showed how these kinds of vicarious stories, stories about other people that resonate with who we are, can promote successful adaptation, help us make good decisions, and teach us morals and values for how to live a good life. We don’t have to experience things directly to learn from them. We can learn from the experiences of others through gossip.

Vicarious stories are particularly prominent in family storytelling. Alongside stories of shared family experiences, such as the Thanksgiving when Dad dropped the turkey on the kitchen floor, and we all had to eat hot dogs, are stories of the family past: stories about parents growing up or grandparents, aunts, and uncles. When the younger generation hears these stories, whether from the person who experienced them (“When I was your age….”) or third-hand as gossip (“Your grandfather loved Thanksgiving, and every year, he would invite friends from work who had nowhere else to go”), these stories become frameworks for how to live a life. Gossip provides us with maps for how the world works.

Of course, there is a dark side to gossip. As Dores-Cruz and colleagues point out, gossip can be used to purposely damage someone else’s reputation, perhaps in the service of self-aggrandizement, and thus can lead to mistrust within the group. They conducted a series of studies to assess people’s motivations and tendency to gossip, especially when the person being gossiped about was experimentally manipulated to be a victim of malicious rumors. They found that group members were more likely to gossip when a group member was being maliciously maligned in order to protect the victim’s reputation. At the same time, people are motivated to spread the word about members of the group who violate norms, suggesting that gossip serves to keep everyone in line. Gossip is a little bit like herding sheep, making sure the group maintains positive bonds and bringing those who deviate from this back into the fold.

This holiday season, there will be gossip! I will spend Thanksgiving with my “framily” (friends and family), and there will be some dear framily we will miss who are not able to be there. But we will gossip! “Did you hear about so-and-so?” and “Let me tell you what happened…” We will laugh, and we will shed tears. And we will cement our bonds. So, this Thanksgiving, if you have something juicy to tell, come sit by me!

Dunbar, R. I. (2004). Gossip in evolutionary perspective. Review of general psychology, 8(2), 100-110.

Williams, K. D., & Nida, S. A. (2022). Ostracism and social exclusion: Implications for separation, social isolation, and loss. Current Opinion in Psychology, 47, 101353.

Pillemer, D. B., Thomsen, D. K., & Fivush, R. (2024). Vicarious memory promotes successful adaptation and enriches the self. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 13(2), 159.

Dores Cruz, T. D., Nieper, A. S., Testori, M., Martinescu, E., & Beersma, B. (2021). An integrative definition and framework to study gossip. Group & Organization Management, 46(2), 252-285.

#4741. Oldest evidence of cannabis use discovered in 2,700-year-old royal tomb

Published Nov 5, 2026 2:00 PM EST

The use of cannabis is documented across cultures stretching back thousands of years, but it frequently relates to harvesting the plant for hemp and other non-psychoactive products. That said, one Bronze Age society of horseriders living in present-day Russia called the Scythians may offer the oldest example of intentionally ingesting cannabis for its intoxicating properties. In the Eurasian steppes of Siberia, archaeologists have discovered a princely Scythian tomb complex featuring an estimated 1,000 cannabis seeds intentionally placed among the dead.

“The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial,” Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern in Switzerland, explained in a statement.

These weren’t simply symbolic objects, either. As Caspari and his colleagues detail in a study published today in the journal Science, human hair samples from the central burial room indicate Scythian royals also partook in cannabis use.

The Scythians were a group of ancient eastern Iranian nomadic equestrians renowned for their horseback skills. The community migrated from Central Asia into present-day Ukraine and southern Russia beginning in the eight and ninth centuries BCE, and stayed there for roughly the next 500 years. Their regional influence eventually waned before the Scythians ultimately assimilating into neighboring populations after being displaced by the Goths during the third century CE.

The burial complex Caspari’s team examined is located in Tuva, a south Siberian republic of Russia located along Mongolia’s northern border. Although ancient plant material like leaves, flowers, and resin generally decompose long before archaeologists can ever locate them, seeds sometimes endure when shielded from the elements. In this case, the royal tomb ensured near optimal conditions to protect the cannabis remnants. Laboratory radiocarbon dating of six recovered seeds indicate Bronze Age attendants likely placed them inside the burial chamber during the early eighth century BCE.

The exact details of Scythian cannabis cultivation and use remains unclear. Researchers theorize the plants were wild variants that naturally grew in the region. At the same time, hair analysis through methods like high-resolution mass spectrometry revealed the clear presence of cannabinol (CBN), which is produced by the oxidation of cannabis’ primary intoxicant, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). The team also noted weak signs consistent with THC itself.

The detection of these molecular signals doesn’t reveal how much cannabis the Scythian royals ingested, or the methods they used. At the same time, other Central Asian archaeological sites contained cannabinoid chemical remnants on heated stones and inside vessels, which strongly suggest inhalation.

“The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave, and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,” concluded Caspari.

Archaeologists are now sequencing the DNA from some of the tomb’s seed samples, which will help them trace the plant’s spread and later human domestication. Cannabis wasn’t the only addition to the royal Scythian tomb, however. Prior work at the site has yielded the skeletal remnants of 18 horses arranged on the burial mound, along with an assortment of human bones.

“In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well,” added Caspari.

#4740. Energica rises from the ashes with plans for cheaper electric motorcycles

The Italian electric motorcycle maker, which ceased operations in 2024 after entering judicial liquidation, has announced a major revival under new international ownership. And while the Energica name is returning, the company behind it is going to look quite different this time around.

Perhaps the biggest change is where the motorcycles will actually be built.

Energica says motorcycle production is moving to Asia, while design, engineering, research and development, as well as responsibility for technical and quality standards, will remain in Italy. The new manufacturing setup is expected to significantly reduce production costs, allowing Energica to cut motorcycle prices by around 20% compared to its previous models.

That could be a big deal for a company whose motorcycles were widely praised for their performance and technology, but were also firmly positioned at the premium end of the market.

The revival comes after Energica was acquired by Energica Pte. Ltd., a Singapore-based company backed by international private investors. Importantly, much of the technological know-how isn’t disappearing overseas with the manufacturing. Energica says its core engineering and design leadership remains in Italy, including longtime CTO Giampiero Testoni and designer Paolo Imeni.

The first motorcycle to make its comeback will be the Energica Experia, the company’s adventure-oriented electric sport-tourer. After that, Energica plans to progressively restart production of the Ego, Eva Ribelle, and EsseEsse9, eventually bringing its entire previous lineup back to market.

At least initially, those motorcycles will use their existing platforms, which should help Energica get bikes rolling off the production line faster without having to develop and homologate entirely new machines. But upgrades are already planned, including a new battery and improvements to range, efficiency, performance, and reliability.

Energica is also specifically targeting Europe, the United States, and Australia as it rebuilds its dealer and service networks. Existing owners haven’t been forgotten either. The company says service has already resumed and spare-parts shipments have restarted to dealers in several countries.

For anyone who followed the electric motorcycle industry over the last decade, Energica’s disappearance was a particularly painful one. This wasn’t some startup with a couple of renderings and a dream. Energica built some of the highest-performance electric motorcycles on the road and spent four seasons supplying the motorcycles for the FIM MotoE World Cup, experience that helped develop its high-voltage and DC fast-charging technology.

Now the company gets something relatively rare in the motorcycle industry: a second chance.

And if moving production to Asia really can knock around 20% off Energica’s prices while retaining the Italian engineering that made the bikes special in the first place, Energica 2.0 might have a considerably better shot at turning great electric motorcycles into a sustainable business.

It seems like moving toward Asian manufacturing is all but inevitable here. It was the expensive European manufacturing of low-volume motorcycles that weighed so heavily on Energica’s balance sheets in the years up to their financial troubles, and so shifting production to countries with both the expertise and the cost benefits for motorcycle manufacturing simply makes sense.

Energica isn’t alone in discovering the economics of moving electric motorcycle production to Asia. Zero Motorcycles spent years manufacturing its bikes in California before beginning a major shift toward production in the Philippines in 2023, including both complete motorcycles and major subassemblies. Now the company works with multiple factories, including major manufacturers like Zongshen in China, to reduce production costs for its electric motorcycles while still maintaining the ‘designed in California’ marketing angle.

It’s too early to tell how the new strategy will play out for Energica, but the fact that the company is now following a more well-worn trail is a positive sign for those who have spent the last two years hoping for a revival.
